name: text-23
text: This study focuses on the time users spend waiting for local code generation.

A local code agent combines a locally running language model with tools such as a test runner. The workflow can avoid sending source code to a remote inference service, provided no remote tools are used. Local execution still needs an appropriate model, and it shares the machine's compute and memory with other applications.

name: text-35
text: Fail: test the revised code again

name: text-40
text: Repair input: task + previous code + test feedback

name: text-42
text: The repair stage generates revised code, then returns to testing.

The user supplies a task. The model generates code and a tool executes visible tests. If a test fails, the repair prompt includes the previous code and its error feedback. The model generates a revised response, and the tool runs tests again. In the evaluated pilot-style workflow, at most two repairs are allowed. Hidden scoring tests never enter the prompt.

name: text-14

name: text-16
text: Optimize inference time. Keep task success and output preservation as separate checks.

This work studies inference latency in local code-agent repair. A model may regenerate unchanged parts of an earlier solution, yet ordinary decoding still processes output sequentially. The goal is to reduce model and agent wall time while preserving the ordinary greedy output in the evaluated runs. This does not claim to repair bugs that the underlying model cannot repair.

name: text-34

name: text-37
text: Long responses still require many sequential model steps.

A token is a small text unit, not necessarily a whole word. In ordinary greedy decoding, the model selects the highest-scoring next token at each step. KV cache stores intermediate attention keys and values for earlier tokens, avoiding recomputation of the full prefix. It does not remove the next-token model steps. The diagram uses text fragments only to explain the sequential process.

name: text-22
text: Batch checking can advance several tokens. A mismatch ends the accepted prefix.

name: text-24
text: Saved target steps must outweigh drafting and verification costs.

Speculative decoding uses cheap draft proposals and a target model that verifies several proposed tokens together. A draft model is usually a smaller and faster model, while the target is the model whose output is desired. This study uses greedy matching: retain the matching prefix and stop accepting at the first mismatch. The original paper also addresses distribution-preserving sampling. Saved target steps must outweigh proposal, verification and other overheads.

text: Agent history and adaptive draft length

name: text-26
text: Our focus: a time-based decision rule for local history drafting, with explicit cost accounting.

Prompt Lookup Decoding retrieves candidate continuations from existing prompt text. EfficientEdit reuses source code and includes edit-oriented drafting and dynamic verification. AgSpec builds retrieval corpora for coding agents and adapts draft length using feedback. DISCO studies dynamic lookahead. The present comparison is against controlled in-project baselines, not reproduced implementations of all these systems. General history reuse and dynamic length are therefore not claimed as first-ever ideas.

name: text-20
text: The proposed component is the action-selection policy, not history lookup itself.

The proposal is a lightweight policy on top of history retrieval and target verification. It scores feasible lengths using estimated time per output token, including verification, lookup and the current implementation's expected recovery. k=0 means ordinary decoding. Its contribution must be argued through this concrete design and controlled evidence, not simply the existence of adaptive length. Cost validation and standard API integration are still pending in this draft.

The history lookup follows an existing n-gram continuation idea. The local implementation matches a recent suffix, retrieves following tokens and caps candidates by available history. It does not access held-out tests. Repair requests use earlier generated code as history; cold first generations take the ordinary path. All controlled history methods share the same retrieval source.

name: text-25

name: text-28
text: Compare the score with ordinary decoding. Select reuse only when it is cheaper.

First ask how much time a step costs and how far it advances the output. C(k) equals estimated verification plus lookup plus expected recovery divided by expected output advance. T_step is the ordinary single-step time. This is a proxy score, not a validated latency predictor. Policy overhead, cache handling and end-of-sequence effects need accounting checks. Offline step and verification calibration are fixed in the current policy; acceptance and lookup estimates update online.

text: On rejection: restore the earlier cache, then recompute the retained prefix through ordinary

name: text-13

name: text-16
text: Replay may be implementation-specific. Check if a correct native path can avoid it.

The current local code snapshots the cache before batched verification. On rejection it restores that snapshot and replays the retained prefix through ordinary single-token forwards. Earlier diagnostics reported shape-related floating-point differences in retained KV values. This explains the implementation choice but is not a universal requirement of speculative decoding. It remains necessary to test whether native cache trimming, a different verification path or another precision avoids replay while preserving complete output. Do not treat replay as a hardware law.

name: text-40
text: Lower score is better. Use a draft only if its estimated cost is at least 5% below ordinary decoding.

name: text-41
text: Assumed inputs explain the rule. They do not validate its predictions.

HYPOTHETICAL DECISION EXAMPLE, NOT AN EXPERIMENT. Use the illustrative V(k) from slide 12, L=0.02 and T_step=1. R(k)=T_step*sum_{j=0}^{k-1}(j+1)*p^j*(1-p), G(k)=1+sum_{j=1}^k p^j. At p=.55 all scores exceed the ordinary path. At p=.9 k4 has the lowest score. At p=.98 k8 has the lowest score. The 5% estimated margin means reuse must score below .95. The calculation assumes geometric acceptance and no truncation. This only explains how the policy operates.

name: text-32
text: The full mlx-lm generation API is a separate planned comparison, not the main engine.

Reported main evaluation uses a custom SiliconLLM synchronous decoding loop based on tiny-llm, with Qwen2-1.5B-Instruct-MLX 4-bit group64 on Apple Silicon with 18 GiB unified memory. Main replay: 30 tasks, 64 fixed requests, three shuffled repetitions. Agent episodes: 20 tasks, three repetitions, up to two repairs, 384 tokens per call. The native extension uses mlx-lm model and cache in a shared synchronous loop. Full stock API integration and timings remain planned. Raw records for the reported external run are not locally available and have not been independently verified here.

Limitations of the adopted results include one hardware/model setting, repeated failed repairs, incomplete access to external raw logs and lack of a full stock API comparison. The thesis examines local inference for agentic repair workloads. It implements a history-based time-scoring policy and controlled comparisons. Reported results show1.45x fixed and1.65x adaptive model speedup on the main queue, and1.62x adaptive agent speedup. These values have limited scope and raw external records remain pending local archiving. The contribution claim must be finalized after cost validation and stock-engine evaluation; hypothetical placeholders do not support it.

name: text-14
text: Check independence, truncation, cache overhead and prediction error before treating C(k) as

The current formula uses a single estimated acceptance probability p and a geometric-prefix approximation. G=1+sum(p^j,j1..k). R/Tstep=sum((j+1)*p^j*(1-p),j0..k-1), matching the assumed rejected-prefix replay but excluding some cache and policy overhead. It is a proxy, not an exact mathematical expectation of implementation latency. Current code acceptance update is .7 old+.3 accepted/proposed; lookup .8 old+.2 observed. k0 only used when no lower score passes5%margin. The feedback variant is distinct. Full acceptance cache-state differences and end-of-sequence truncation require explicit correctness checks.
